rv.q: There's some overlap here with 2015's Motown: The Musical, which covered a broader swath of the legendary hit factory's history. But this is the superior show, less pedestrian in its storytelling, if not without its own limitations.
That’s the urge being translated with such sublime grace by those five natty men on the stage, Platonic ideals of stepping high and looking fine.

That it does, as it centers on the story of the classic quintet of performers singing "Cloud Nine," "If You Don't Know Me By Now," "My Girl," "I'm Gonna Make You Love Me" and the title song, among others — including some songs that weren't the group's own.

You're left wishing the show had chosen one part of this band's life and stayed close therein, found more real-time dramatic action and, above all, been more willing to look at America through this astonishing catalog of musical greatness.

Ain't Too Proud mostly accomplishes what so many of the lesser examples of this genre haven't – a fine cast performs beloved songs, performs them well enough to conjure and honor the people they're playing.

Instead the script delivers clichés and melodrama, with founding member and sole surviving singer of the original group Otis Williams (Derrick Baskin) earnestly delivering a kind of "Behind the Music" narration.
The new musical about the Temptations is slick and entertaining, but it doesn't dig deep enough into the group's story or the social context that shaped their music.
But underneath its sparkle is a theatrical monotony that drags the whole thing down.
For the songs, of course, and the undiluted pleasure of watching five superb singers and dancers perform them.
As musical theater, Ain’t Too Proud could generously be described as shameless.
As for Dominique Morisseau’s book, it sounds as though a roomful of ad executives wrote it.

Ain’t Too Proud is a stellar production that elevates the quality of jukebox musicals with its engaging story and direction, top-notch performances, sophisticated design, and a selection of high-voltage choreographed hits that keeps the legacy of Motown alive and ‘Temptation strutting.’
This jukebox musical not only has life, it also has wit, intelligence, while also looking stunning and full of energy.
Morisseau's well-crafted storytelling proves just as important as the musical memories.
What makes Beg memorable is the sheer overwhelming talent of the cast.

"Jersey Boys" meets "Motown" in "Ain't Too Proud: The Life and Times of The Temptations," the latest biographical/backstage rock and roll jukebox musical to hit Broadway and market itself to the baby-boomer demographic. And while not exactly profound or original, it makes for slick, straightforward, tuneful and altogether pleasant entertainment.
The show works best when it lets the music do the talking, and the Temptations' catalog is more than up to the task of carrying the evening.
He only got his girlfriend pregnant, endured a shotgun wedding and promptly ignored his wife before she left him for another man. Years later, his only son died in a construction accident at age 22.
Even with an unoriginal, decades-spanning, episodic book, they’re gonna make you love them (oh, yes, they will).

If none of the virtuosic performances in Ain’t Too Proud match the effortless sweetness and soulfulness of the original recordings, the abundance of talent and energy onstage is something to marvel at in its own right.
Proud this show is — but distinctive, it ain’t.

cn.t: Critics find this Temptations jukebox musical slick and entertaining with electrifying performances and irresistible hits, but fault its conventional, superficial storytelling that fails to match the depth of its music.

sg.ra: Imperial's auditorium is rectangular and wider than it is deep, so you lose very little distance moving back from the premium C-G band — and once you clear the mezzanine overhang (which hangs over Orchestra row H) the rake picks up enough to see over heads. Multiple Chess (2026) and Water for Elephants (2024) sitters in rows H-P described a dead-center full-stage view at sub-premium prices; one Chess viewer at Orch C H106 called it 'the best broadway seats I've had.' Seatplan, TickPick, and Headout independently pick this same band as the value tier.

TickPick and Seatplan both explicitly recommend Front Mezz row C and back (centered) over rows A-B, because the Imperial's front-mezz railing sits high enough to clip the stage for front-row sitters — a Water for Elephants viewer at Front Mezz R A401 (self-reported 6'3") wrote 'The bar definitely gets in the way… Avoid.' Rows C-F clear that bar while keeping the whole-stage overhead view that's the main reason to choose mezzanine over orchestra at Imperial.

sg.vl: Steep rake saves the cheap seats
sg.ra: Imperial has no elevators/escalators and the rear mezz is a real climb (one Chess sitter called it 'quite the hike'), but the rake is steep enough that several Chess and Smash viewers reported unobstructed full-stage views from rows A-C even with tall people in front ('Rake is good so most likely no heads blocking the stage,' 'Theater has a good rake so you can see over the person in front of you'). TickPick and Headout both specifically recommend rear-mezz center (not sides) as the cheap-seat sweet spot here.

sg.vl: Under the overhang, far from the action
sg.ra: Imperial is wider than it is deep, so the penalty for sitting far back is real — you lose closeness without gaining much sightline, and the same mid-tier price bracket gets you a few rows forward.
